close_reason: Added DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=30s to UreqFetcher::new() and ReqwestFetcher::new(). with_agent/with_client escape hatches preserved.
description:
src/clients/reqwest.rs:52 and src/clients/ureq.rs:51: `ReqwestFetcher::new()` uses `::reqwest::Client::new()`; `UreqFetcher::new()` uses `::ureq::agent()`. Neither sets a connect timeout, read timeout, or per-request total timeout. `reqwest::Client::new()` explicitly defaults to no timeout; `ureq::agent()` likewise.

Trigger: a certificate's cRLDistributionPoints or AIA OCSP URL points at a slowloris responder (attacker-controlled or simply broken). pkix-revocation-http calls fetch(); the underlying client hangs indefinitely (or until kernel TCP keepalive fires, minutes-to-hours).

Bad behavior: `check_revocation` does not return. In a path-validator wired into a TLS server, this hangs the TLS handshake for the offending client cert. In a batch validation job, the worker stalls. The certificate's contents — including the AIA/CDP URL — are attacker-controlled in many threat models (S/MIME signer cert from untrusted source, client cert mutual-TLS from an attacker, etc.).

The crate-level Limitations docstring says 'No retry / backoff policy'. That is not the same as 'no default timeout' — a missing timeout is a sharper footgun than a missing retry policy because a missing timeout is a liveness bug, not a robustness one.

Fix: ship sane defaults on both reference clients (e.g. 30s connect, 60s read, 90s total). Document the value. Allow override via with_timeout / with_agent / with_client. Document in the crate-level Limitations that callers building their own RevocationFetcher MUST impose a timeout.

This is the kind of footgun where the reference implementation in a published crate becomes the de-facto default — copy-paste from the rustdoc example into production, no timeout, CVE.
title: Reference HTTP clients have no default timeouts → remote DoS via malicious AIA/CDP URLs
